title: Near-linear incremental topological ordering
formal:
Does there exist one uniform Las Vegas randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A\) that maintains a topological order of an initially empty directed graph on \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), under edge insertions promised to preserve acyclicity, with all the following guarantees? Order-comparison queries take \(O(1)\) worst-case time, space is \(O((n+m)(\log_2(n+2))^C)\) words for one fixed \(C\ge0\), and for every real \(\eta>0\) there is a constant \(K_\eta>0\) such that
\[
\mathbb E[\text{initialization and update instructions through any prefix}]
\le K_\eta(n+m)^{1+\eta}.
\]
Here \(m\) is the number of insertions in that prefix, and \(n\ge2\). The same algorithm must meet all exponents; \(q\) comparison queries add at most \(K_Qq\) instructions for one absolute constant \(K_Q\).
definitions:
The input begins with \(n\). An insertion supplies an ordered pair \((u,v)\) with \(u\ne v\) whose directed edge is not already present. There are no loops, repeated insertions or deletions. Every prefix graph is promised to have no directed cycle. No requirement is imposed on operations violating this promise. The algorithm is online: it is not given future edges or the final edge count. Any finite insertion/query sequence must be handled; that sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm's random choices.

After initialization and each insertion the algorithm must represent some strict total order \(\prec\) of all \(n\) vertices such that \(u\prec v\) for every present edge \((u,v)\). A query on vertices \(u,v\) returns the bit indicating \(u\prec v\), including zero when \(u=v\). Every query between two successive insertions refers to the same maintained order. The algorithm may choose a new valid total order at an insertion. It need not enumerate the entire order after each change, and a comparison is not a reachability query. Every returned answer and maintained order must be correct; initialization and insertions terminate almost surely. Queries terminate within their fixed worst-case instruction bound on every random tape.

The RAM has one finite program, word registers and word-addressed memory. For some fixed integer constant \(a\ge3\) chosen with the algorithm, a word has \(w=a\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits. One instruction may copy, read or write an addressed word, compare, branch, perform Boolean bit operations or logical shifts, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or compute integer quotient or remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts of at least \(w\) bits return zero. Addresses must fit a word; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. An instruction may generate one independent uniform random word. There is no advice, free table or input-dependent oracle. All initialization, allocation, preprocessing, retained graph data, temporary workspace and random seeds count toward time or space as appropriate.

The memory bound applies on every execution, including temporary workspace during an operation, with \(m\) counting edges submitted through that operation. One fixed constant bounds space uniformly over all inputs and prefixes. The expected-time bound includes initialization and every insertion in the selected prefix; it averages the algorithm's private randomness on the fixed operation sequence. Each \(K_\eta\) is independent of \(n,m,q\) and the sequence. It may depend on \(\eta\) and the one chosen algorithm. There is no amortized cost charged against a future insertion not yet present in the prefix, and no extra additive bound depending on the final sequence length. Query instructions are charged separately by the displayed linear bound. Thus the target is total update time \((n+m)^{1+o(1)}\), not necessarily \(O((n+m)\operatorname{polylog} n)\).

No prediction of the update sequence, special graph class, computational conjecture or additional source of randomness is supplied. The full stated RAM instruction set is allowed; an undefined restriction to combinatorial algorithms is not part of this question.
why: Maintaining an actual vertex order remains a central gap between static graph processing and incremental graph maintenance, even as cycle detection itself has become almost linear.

context_blocks.text: Static topological ordering is linear in graph size. Maintaining an actual order online requires handling edges that contradict the current order while remaining consistent with all earlier edges.
The source records soft-\(O(n^2)\) dense and soft-\(O(m^{4/3})\) sparse bounds. It explicitly says that the almost-linear cycle-detection breakthrough does not maintain an order.
The 2026 prediction-based SCC paper retains this distinction. Its faster performance when the predicted sequence is accurate depends on information absent from the selected target.

progress.text: The seminar describes the gap between fast cycle detection and actual incremental topological ordering; its stated combinatorial improvement is a separate milestone.
The SWAT paper compares dense and sparse order-based methods with almost-linear SCC maintenance without an order, and gives prediction-assisted guarantees in a different input model.

answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this existence claim or its logical negation. A positive answer must use one algorithm for every \(\eta>0\), preserve the promised order and constant worst-case comparisons, and prove the stated prefix expectation and memory bounds. A family choosing a different algorithm for each fixed exponent, near-linear cycle detection without an order, or a prediction-dependent speedup does not establish this target. A negative answer must refute the full allowed randomized RAM claim; failure of one method or a conjecture-based lower bound alone is insufficient.

sentences: Directed edges arrive online while every prefix graph remains acyclic.
The algorithm must maintain a total vertex order consistent with all current edges.
Queries compare vertices in that order with constant worst-case cost.
The target combines almost-linear expected total update time with near-linear storage.
Known fast cycle detection and prediction-assisted maintenance do not supply the selected unassisted ordering guarantee.
